article.headline: Historic AI Infrastructure Spending Leaves Energy as the Overlooked Trade
article.lede: Ronald-Peter Stöferle, managing partner of Incrementum AG and author of the widely-cited annual 'In Gold We Trust' report, packages a striking historical comparison and a market-positioning trade into a single post. The AI infrastructure buildout, he argues, represents the largest concentrated capital mobilization in American history — and the market has priced the technology stack while leaving the physical infrastructure to power it nearly unowned.
article.body:
The chart at the center of this post compares planned AI *data center* *capex* — physical spending on servers, cooling, and power by Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta Platforms (META), and Oracle (ORCL) — against the inflation-adjusted cost of great American megaprojects. The underlying numbers are credible: Epoch AI, which extracts standardized figures directly from SEC filings, estimates the five *hyperscalers* spent roughly $500 billion on infrastructure in 2025 alone, with 2026 *forward guidance* pushing combined commitments past $700 billion. A six-year cumulative total near $930 billion is plausible under reasonable definitions of the time window and which companies to include.

The specific claim that this sum exceeds the Marshall Plan, Apollo Program, Manhattan Project, and Interstate Highway System *combined* is, however, sensitive to inflation methodology — and the chart's own figures create a problem. Its stated figures ($170 billion for the Marshall Plan, $252 billion for Apollo, $36 billion for the Manhattan Project, and $620 billion for the Interstate) sum to roughly **$1.08 trillion**, which is larger than $930 billion, not smaller. The claim holds only under more conservative inflation adjustments that peg the Interstate at around $500 billion and the Marshall Plan near $130 billion, yielding a combined figure of about $880 billion. Neither interpretation is obviously wrong — inflation methodology is a legitimate variable — but as presented, the tweet overstates the comparison against the chart's own numbers. The broader narrative — that this cycle is mobilizing capital at a pace without peacetime precedent — stands on its own without the contested arithmetic.

The more original observation is the equity-positioning argument. Information Technology and Communication Services together represent roughly 43 percent of the S&P 500 by *sector weight* — the sectors containing the hyperscalers, the *GPU* supply chain, and the software platforms built atop AI. **Energy** represents approximately 4 percent. The ratio is about eleven to one. Stöferle's thesis is that markets have bid up the consumers of electricity while largely ignoring the producers and distributors of it.

The demand case for energy is well-grounded. The International Energy Agency reported in early 2026 that global data center electricity consumption surged 17 percent in 2025, with AI-focused facilities accounting for roughly half of that growth. AI data center power use is projected to triple by 2030. New data center construction currently in progress could add 140 gigawatts of load to the grid — approximately ten times current data center consumption. Hyperscalers are already shifting from passive utility customers to active partners in power generation, negotiating private nuclear and natural-gas agreements precisely because the grid cannot absorb demand at the rate they require.

Stöferle's prior is relevant context. As an Austrian School economist and a vocal gold and Bitcoin advocate, his analytical lens consistently favors real assets over financial claims — and the energy trade fits that worldview neatly. The thesis does not depend on his authority alone: Morgan Stanley (MS) and BlackRock (BLK) have published substantially similar energy-bottleneck arguments in 2026, and the IEA's demand data is primary evidence independent of any investor's prior. The question this post actually raises — whether equity markets are systematically underpricing physical constraints on digital growth — is a serious one, whatever one thinks of the messenger.

concepts.definition: Money a company spends on physical long-term assets — servers, buildings, power equipment — rather than day-to-day operating costs. In the AI buildout context, capex tracks how much hyperscalers are investing in the physical infrastructure that runs AI models, and is reported in SEC filings and quarterly earnings.

A cloud computing company that operates data centers at a scale large enough to achieve significant cost efficiencies and reshape adjacent markets — typically Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle. The term implies sufficient bargaining power to move electricity prices, real estate markets, and chip supply chains.

Originally designed for rendering video game graphics, GPUs are now the dominant hardware for training and running AI models because their massively parallel architecture handles the matrix mathematics of neural networks far more efficiently than conventional CPUs. Nvidia supplies the dominant share of AI GPUs.

The proportion of a stock market index — such as the S&P 500 — represented by companies classified in a given industry sector. A sector weight of 43 percent for technology means 43 cents of every dollar invested in the index goes to technology companies. Weights shift automatically as market capitalizations change.

Company-issued statements about expected future financial performance, typically shared during quarterly earnings calls. Capital expenditure guidance is closely watched in the AI sector because it signals how aggressively a company plans to invest in infrastructure over the coming year, and often moves related stocks — chip makers, utilities, real estate investment trusts — on publication.

A unit of power equal to one billion watts, used to describe large-scale electricity generation and consumption. A single gigawatt can power roughly 750,000 average American homes. Modern hyperscale AI data centers can consume one gigawatt or more each — a scale that strains regional power grids built over decades for far smaller loads.

A tradition in economic thought, associated with economists including Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, that emphasizes the role of individual action, skepticism of central bank intervention, and preference for hard-money assets like gold over paper or credit-based wealth. Investors in this tradition tend to favor commodities and real assets as hedges against monetary expansion.

article.fact_check: The tweet claims the six-year AI data center capex of approximately $930 billion exceeds the combined inflation-adjusted cost of the Marshall Plan, Apollo Program, Manhattan Project, and Interstate Highway System. The claim is contestable on its own chart's numbers. The chart assigns those four programs $170 billion, $252 billion, $36 billion, and $620 billion respectively — a sum of roughly $1.08 trillion, which is larger than $930 billion, not smaller. The tweet's claim holds only under more conservative inflation adjustments (Interstate at ~$500 billion, Marshall Plan at ~$130 billion), yielding a combined total of roughly $880 billion. Inflation methodology is a genuine variable and neither the high nor low estimates are wrong per se, but the tweet presents the comparison as settled when it is sensitive to which deflator is applied. The broader narrative — that this investment cycle is historically unprecedented in pace — is supported by Epoch AI's SEC-filing data and does not require the 'exceeds all combined' framing to be persuasive.

ticker_amzn.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
ticker_amzn.blurb: Amazon operates the world's largest e-commerce marketplace and the leading cloud infrastructure platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS). AWS generates the majority of Amazon's operating profit despite representing a minority of total revenue. The company also has significant positions in digital advertising, streaming (Prime Video), and logistics infrastructure. Amazon is a major investor in AI, both through AWS cloud AI services and through a multi-billion-dollar strategic stake in Anthropic.
ticker_amzn.recent: Amazon reported FY2025 revenue exceeding $650 billion, with AWS growing at roughly 17% annually and crossing $100 billion in run-rate revenue. The advertising segment has become a meaningful profit contributor. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026), with the stock gaining approximately 10% over that period — the weakest performer in the Pelosi 2026 exercise batch.

ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.

ticker_meta.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
ticker_meta.blurb: Meta Platforms, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — collectively the largest social-media ecosystem in the world by monthly active users. The company generates the vast majority of its revenue through digital advertising, using detailed behavioural data to target ads across its platforms. After a painful 2022 in which shares fell roughly 65% amid a revenue slowdown and ballooning metaverse losses, Meta executed a dramatic turnaround by cutting costs, boosting margins, and rapidly integrating AI-driven ad ranking tools (Advantage+) that demonstrably improved advertiser returns. CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'Year of Efficiency' and the company followed through. By late 2025 Meta was simultaneously the most profitable it had ever been and the most aggressive in AI infrastructure spending, committing up to $65 billion in capex for 2025 and raising that figure to as much as $145 billion for 2026.
ticker_meta.recent: Meta reached an all-time high near $796 per share in September 2025. The stock declined approximately 24–28% from that peak through April 2026, with the primary investor concern being the scale of the 2026 capital-expenditure commitment — up to $145 billion — and uncertainty about whether AI-driven revenue would materialise at the pace required to justify it. Quarterly earnings remained strong through the period, but multiple compression drove share-price weakness.

ticker_orcl.name: Oracle Corporation
ticker_orcl.blurb: Oracle is an enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company founded by Larry Ellison in 1977 and headquartered in Austin, Texas. Its core businesses are database software (Oracle Database remains the dominant enterprise RDBMS by revenue), cloud applications (ERP, HCM, and CX via Oracle Fusion and NetSuite), and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), its IaaS platform. OCI entered the AI infrastructure race later than AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud but has emerged as a preferred hyperscale partner for OpenAI and other large AI workloads, partly due to competitive GPU pricing and multi-region data-centre commitments. Oracle is an equity participant in the Stargate joint venture alongside OpenAI and SoftBank.
ticker_orcl.recent: Oracle's fiscal Q3 2026 (ending February 2026) was described by management as the strongest quarter in more than 15 years: total revenue rose 22% year-on-year to $17.2 billion, cloud revenue jumped 44% to $8.9 billion, and GPU-related cloud revenue grew 177% year-on-year in the prior quarter. The company reported a $523 billion remaining performance-obligation backlog — driven by AI mega-deals with OpenAI and Meta — and committed approximately $50 billion in capital expenditure for fiscal 2026. BNP Paribas analysts estimated that Oracle's 4.5 gigawatt Stargate capacity commitment could eventually generate $30–60 billion in annual revenue.

poster_ronstoeferle.blurb: Ronnie Stoeferle is a fund manager at Incrementum AG in Liechtenstein, best known as the author of the annual 'In Gold We Trust' report, a widely-read institutional research publication on gold and sound money. He is also co-author of 'Austrian School for Investors,' applying Austrian economics to investing. He posts primarily about gold, Bitcoin, macro economics, and monetary policy, and co-launched what he describes as the world's first fund combining physical gold with Bitcoin. His follower count is not confirmed from available sources.
poster_ronstoeferle.credibility_note: Stoeferle is a prominent gold bull with a long-standing public track record via the annual 'In Gold We Trust' report; his views carry a known pro-gold, pro-hard-money bias rooted in Austrian economics. No major public corrections or controversies were found in the available sources.
